body:
The society of the Harappan civilisation

The Harappan or Indus civilisation was one of the earliest urban civilisations of the Indian subcontinent. Its Mature Harappan phase flourished approximately between 2600 BCE and 1900 BCE. Its settlements extended across a large region that included parts of present-day Pakistan and northwestern India, including Gujarat.

Harappan society included farmers, herders, craftspersons, traders and people involved in organising settlements and economic activities. Large cities such as Harappa and Mohenjodaro depended on agricultural settlements for food and on specialised workers for pottery, ornaments, tools, construction and other goods.

The presence of planned cities, specialised occupations, long-distance trade and standardised objects indicates a complex society. However, the precise organisation of families, social groups, political authority and religious institutions remains uncertain.

How do we know about Harappan life?

Most information about Harappan society comes from physical remains rather than readable historical records. Houses, streets, pottery, ornaments, seals, figurines and graves provide evidence of different aspects of everyday life.

These objects reveal what people made, used and sometimes valued. They do not always reveal the beliefs, social positions or personal identities of their owners.

What physical remains tell us

  • Houses and household objects: Reveal residential arrangements, domestic activities and differences in living conditions.
  • Tools and craft objects: Indicate specialised occupations and the production of goods.
  • Ornaments and valuable materials: Provide clues about differences in access to resources.
  • Seals and standardised weights: Suggest organised exchange and widely shared practices.
  • Figurines and unusual structures: Provide possible evidence of symbolic or ritual activities.
  • Burials: Reveal some customs concerning the treatment of the dead.

The importance of the undeciphered script

The Harappans possessed a writing system. Signs occur on seals, tablets, pottery, tools and other objects. A particularly important example from Gujarat is the large Harappan signboard discovered at Dholavira.

Most Harappan inscriptions are very short. The script contains approximately 375 to 400 different signs according to the classification presented in NCERT. The direction of writing was commonly from right to left.

The Harappan script remains undeciphered. No proposed reading has achieved general scholarly acceptance. Consequently, historians cannot confidently identify the language of the inscriptions, the names of Harappan rulers or the names of their deities from these signs.

This limitation is especially important when examining political and religious interpretations. An image may appear to represent a ruler or deity, but without a securely understood inscription, its identity cannot be established merely from resemblance.

Evidence is not the same as interpretation

The discovery of a seated figure on a seal is an established fact. Identifying that figure as a particular deity is an interpretation. Similarly, planned cities demonstrate organised activity, but do not directly establish the existence of a particular king or form of government.

Degrees of certainty

Harappan society is best understood by distinguishing securely established features from reasonable possibilities and unresolved questions.

AspectEstablished evidenceUnresolved question
Domestic lifeHouses, courtyards and bathing areasExact family organisation
Social differencesVariation in houses and valuable objectsPrecise social hierarchy
Political authorityPlanning and standardisationIdentity and number of rulers
ReligionFigurines, symbolic images and possible ritual structuresNames of deities and beliefs
BurialGraves and associated objectsExact beliefs about death

The distinction matters because an archaeological object can support several possible interpretations. A reliable understanding retains the evidence without treating every proposed explanation as a proven fact.

Prelims focus

  • The Mature Harappan civilisation flourished approximately between 2600 BCE and 1900 BCE.
  • Houses, seals, figurines, ornaments and graves are important sources for understanding Harappan society.
  • The Harappan script remains undeciphered.
  • Most inscriptions are short and commonly appear on seals and other objects.
  • The exact political organisation and religious beliefs of the Harappans remain uncertain.
  • Trap: The existence of writing does not mean that Harappan written records can currently be read.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Theme 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation, pp. 1, 15–17 and 22–24; NCERT, Class 6, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Chapter 6, The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation, pp. 98–101.]

title: Understanding Harappan Society: Evidence and Uncertainty

body:
Residential life in Harappan cities

The residential buildings of Mohenjodaro provide important evidence about Harappan domestic life. Many houses were constructed around a central courtyard, with rooms opening towards it.

The courtyard probably served as a place for activities such as cooking, weaving and other household work. In a hot climate, this arrangement provided an open space within the house while allowing surrounding rooms to be used for different purposes.

Many houses also display architectural arrangements that suggest concern for privacy. At Mohenjodaro, entrances were often positioned so that a person standing outside could not directly see the interior courtyard. Ground-level walls facing the street generally lacked windows.

These features suggest that the internal activities of households were partly separated from public street life.

Bathing, water and domestic facilities

A distinctive feature of Harappan residential architecture was the provision of bathing facilities.

  • Many houses at Mohenjodaro possessed brick-paved bathing areas.
  • Domestic wastewater could pass through drains connected to larger street drains.
  • Some houses contained wells, while others obtained water from nearby sources.
  • Several houses had staircases, indicating access to roofs or upper storeys.

These features demonstrate attention to water use and household cleanliness. They also suggest that bathing was an ordinary domestic activity, rather than something confined to special public structures.

What do houses reveal about family organisation?

A house provides evidence of residential arrangements, but its plan does not reveal the complete structure of the family living within it.

For example, several rooms around a courtyard could have accommodated members of a large household. However, the arrangement does not establish whether the occupants formed a joint family, a nuclear family or some other residential group.

Similarly, the presence of cooking areas and domestic tools cannot establish which members of the household performed particular activities.

Household and family are not identical concepts. A household refers to people sharing a residential and domestic arrangement. A family refers to relationships such as kinship and marriage. The surviving architecture provides stronger evidence about households than about exact family relationships.

Occupations and the division of work

Harappan settlements depended on different kinds of work. Farmers and herders produced food, while specialised craftspersons manufactured pottery, beads, ornaments, tools and other goods.

Craft activities could take place in individual houses or specialised workshops. The presence of tools, unfinished objects and finished products indicates that some individuals developed considerable skill in particular occupations.

Harappan society also included people engaged in exchange and transport. The widespread use of seals suggests the existence of people who could prepare or use inscribed objects, although the extent of literacy is unknown.

Women, men and domestic work

Spindle whorls, pottery, ornaments and other household objects provide evidence of spinning, food preparation and personal adornment. However, these objects do not by themselves reveal a fixed division of labour between women and men.

For example, the discovery of a spindle whorl demonstrates that thread was spun. It does not establish that spinning was performed exclusively by women.

Similarly, figurines depicting women cannot establish the legal position, property rights or social status of women in Harappan society.

Children and everyday activities

Terracotta toy carts, animal figures, rattles and other objects indicate the presence of play and recreation. Such finds help reconstruct ordinary social life beyond agriculture, trade and major public buildings.

These objects show that Harappan settlements contained a range of domestic and recreational activities. Their precise users and social meanings, however, cannot always be identified.

Prelims focus

  • Many Mohenjodaro houses were arranged around a central courtyard.
  • Rooms commonly opened towards the courtyard.
  • House entrances often prevented a direct view into the interior.
  • Brick-paved bathing areas and connections to street drains were important domestic features.
  • Spindle whorls provide evidence of spinning.
  • Trap: Domestic objects do not establish that particular occupations were performed exclusively by men or women.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Theme 1, Section 3.2, Domestic Architecture, pp. 7–8, and Section 11.2, Problems of Interpretation, pp. 23–24; NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts-I, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, pp. 35–40; NCERT, Class 6, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Chapter 6, pp. 91–94 and 100–101.]

title: Homes, Households and Everyday Work

body:
Meaning of social differentiation

Social differentiation refers to differences among individuals or groups within a society. These differences may involve occupation, wealth, access to resources, social position or responsibilities.

The Harappan civilisation possessed specialised occupations, settlements of different sizes and objects of unequal value. These features suggest that the population was not completely uniform in its economic circumstances.

However, differences in wealth do not automatically establish the existence of a rigid caste system, hereditary social classes or a particular political hierarchy.

Ordinary objects and valuable objects

One way to understand economic differences is to compare widely distributed objects of everyday use with objects made from rare materials or requiring specialised production.

Objects of everyday use

Common household objects included pottery, grinding stones, needles and other practical tools. Many were manufactured using relatively accessible materials such as clay and stone.

The widespread occurrence of these objects indicates that similar basic activities were carried out in many households.

Rare and valuable objects

Objects made from gold, semi-precious stones or technically demanding materials were less common. Their distribution provides clues about unequal access to valuable goods.

An important example is faience, an artificially produced material made from ground sand or silica with binding and colouring substances, which was shaped and fired. It could be used for beads, ornaments and small vessels.

Miniature faience vessels were concentrated particularly in major settlements such as Mohenjodaro and Harappa. NCERT notes that such vessels were not found at smaller Kalibangan in the evidence it discusses.

This distribution suggests that particular valuable objects were more readily available in major urban centres.

Gold ornaments and hoards

Gold was rare in the Harappan archaeological record and was probably considered valuable.

In the finds discussed in NCERT, gold jewellery was recovered from hoards rather than ordinary graves. A hoard is a collection of objects deliberately stored or concealed and not subsequently retrieved.

This distinction is important. A hoard is not necessarily a burial offering, and the discovery of valuable objects does not automatically establish that they belonged to rulers.

Differences in housing

Harappan houses varied in size and internal arrangement. Larger houses could provide more space and facilities, while smaller houses offered more limited accommodation.

The variation is compatible with differences in wealth or household requirements, but house size alone cannot establish the social rank of the occupants.

At Dholavira in Gujarat, the fortified Castle, Middle Town and Lower Town contained residential and other structures of different proportions and quality. These features provide stronger evidence of a differentiated urban society.

The settlement's spatial organisation indicates that different parts of the population may have occupied distinct residential areas. Nevertheless, the precise social identities and responsibilities associated with those areas are not fully known.

Burial evidence and social status

Harappan graves sometimes contained ornaments, pottery or copper objects. Certain burial pits were also constructed differently from others.

These variations might reflect social differences, but Harappan cemeteries generally do not display the enormous concentrations of wealth associated with some royal burials in other ancient civilisations.

Jewellery has been recovered from burials of both men and women. Therefore, the presence of jewellery cannot by itself identify a burial as female.

What can be concluded?

Differences in houses, valuable objects and settlement organisation support the existence of economic and possibly social inequalities. They do not establish a particular caste system, hereditary elite or known ruling dynasty.

Occupation and status are different

A craft specialist could possess highly developed skills without necessarily occupying a high political position. Likewise, a trader who handled valuable goods was not automatically a ruler.

The evidence establishes occupational specialisation more securely than it establishes a fixed ranking of occupations.

Therefore, statements about the existence of different occupations are better supported than statements assigning specific castes or hereditary privileges to those occupations.

Prelims focus

  • Social differentiation may involve wealth, occupation, resources and social position.
  • Ordinary pottery and tools were more widely distributed than rare luxury objects.
  • Faience was an artificially produced material used for ornaments and small vessels.
  • Miniature faience vessels were especially associated with large centres such as Mohenjodaro and Harappa.
  • Gold jewellery in the Harappan finds discussed by NCERT came from hoards.
  • Dholavira provides evidence of spatial differentiation within an urban settlement.
  • Trap: Differences in wealth do not prove the existence of a specific caste system.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Theme 1, Section 4, Tracking Social Differences, pp. 9–10; NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Chapter 2, Arts of the Indus Valley, pp. 13–15; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Dholavira: a Harappan City, Brief Synthesis and Statement of Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: Social Differentiation: Wealth and Status
